title: The Lady of Shalott
source: Tate Britain, London, N01543, presented by Sir Henry Tate 1894 (public domain). Wikimedia Commons file: John William Waterhouse - The Lady of Shalott - Google Art Project.jpg (4180 x 3208 px; Tate N01543 via Google Arts & Culture)
caption: She was cursed never to look outside. Then one knight rode by. Would you have looked? #tragedy #poetry #preraphaelite #fineart #storytime
_verify: VERIFIED 2026-10-28, Wikipedia EN (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lady_of_Shalott_(painting)): oil on canvas, 1888, Tate Britain, given by Sir Henry Tate in 1894; based on Tennyson's poem; under the curse she could see the outside world only through a mirror; when Lancelot passes the mirror cracks and the curse falls; crucifix near the bow with three candles beside it, two blown out (death soon to come); lantern at the front of the boat; she sits on the tapestry she has woven; she sings a lament as she sails to Camelot; naturalistic river details (water plants, swallows).

VERIFIED, Tate (tate.org.uk/art/artists/john-william-waterhouse-583/curse-lady-shalott): 'Forbidden to leave, she can only see the outside world through the reflection in a mirror'; she 'glimpses the handsome knight Lancelot in the mirror, her curse is fulfilled'; 'a crucifix symbolizing sacrifice and three candles', two gone out; 'Draped over the boat is the tapestry illustrating the Lady herself and Lancelot surrounded by other knights'. Tate artwork page: tate.org.uk/art/artworks/waterhouse-the-lady-of-shalott-n01543.

VERIFIED, Tennyson, The Lady of Shalott, 1842 text (rpo.library.utoronto.ca/poems/lady-shalott-1842): 'There she weaves by night and day / A magic web'; 'A curse is on her if she stay / To look down to Camelot'; she 'knows not what the curse may be'; 'The mirror crack'd from side to side; / "The curse is come upon me," cried'; 'She loosed the chain'; 'Singing in her song she died'. The quote on slide 5 is the poem's own line.

VERIFIED with nuance, painted outdoors: Art UK (artuk.org, The Lady of Shalott 117690) says it was made during Waterhouse's brief period of plein-air painting, landscape 'highly naturalistic', exact location not identified; HASTA St Andrews: 'Painting en plein-air'; Smarthistory: Waterhouse drew on the 'plein air (open air) methods of the Impressionists'. Slide 9 says only 'painted in the open air', no river named. UNVERIFIED, not used: which river (Somerset/Devon guesses only).

CAUTIOUS: 'her lips are parted' on slide 8 is a visual description (painting shows the mouth slightly open); the singing is from the poem and Wikipedia. Death is implied, never described ('her song ends before she arrives').
CONFLICTING, not used: dimensions (Wikipedia 183 x 230 cm; Art UK 153 x 200 cm). Model 'traditionally said to be the artist's wife' (Art UK): not used.

CAUTIOUS: slide 4 says only 'This is her tapestry' (Tate: draped over the boat, shows the Lady and Lancelot among knights). Slide 5 follows the poem: she sees Lancelot in the mirror, leaves the web and looks down to Camelot; 'straight at him' is a light simplification.
Focus boxes are estimates from memory of the composition (landscape, about 1.26-1.31 width/height; prow with lantern, crucifix and candles at left); re-tune on the real image.
2026-10-28 laptop, slide 1 text changed after checking the image: "in a boat, alone, toward a distant castle." -> "in a boat, alone.". No castle is visible in the painting.

slides.headline: She was cursed never to look.
slides.sub: John William Waterhouse, The Lady of Shalott, 1888

slides.headline: Alone on the river
slides.text: Waterhouse, 1888. A woman drifts downstream in a boat, alone. Who is she, and why does she look so lost?

slides.headline: The Lady of Shalott
slides.text: She comes from Tennyson's poem. Locked in a tower, she wove day and night, under a curse she didn't even understand.

slides.headline: A world in a mirror
slides.text: The rule: never look out at Camelot. She saw the world only in a mirror, and wove what it showed. This is her tapestry.

slides.headline: Then, Lancelot
slides.text: Then a knight rode by: Lancelot. She left the mirror and looked out, straight at him. The mirror cracked. "The curse is come upon me."

slides.headline: She lets go
slides.text: So she left her tower, found a boat by the river, and climbed in. Look at her hands: she is loosing the chain.

slides.headline: Three candles
slides.text: Look closer at the prow: a crucifix and three candles. Two have already gone out. Only one flame still flickers. Time is running out.

slides.headline: Her last song
slides.text: And her lips are parted. In the poem, she sings as the boat drifts toward Camelot, and her song ends before she arrives.

slides.headline: One glance
slides.text: Waterhouse painted in the open air, so reeds, swallows and water feel alive. Only she is fading. Would you have risked that glance?
